appraisal_events.evidence: Unlike her performed enthusiasm elsewhere, 'c'est en toute sincérité qu'elle regardait le salon de la duchesse de Guermantes comme un lieu privilégié où elle ne pouvait marcher que de surprises en délices,' persuaded that everything there was of superior quality.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator explicitly marks the princess's admiration for the duchesse's household as genuine rather than performed, elevating the duchesse's household as a benchmark of superior taste.

appraisal_events.evidence: Drawing on the Louis XIV analogy of ceremonial devotion overriding real feeling, the narrator finds intact in M. de Guermantes, 'homme attendrissant de gentillesse et révoltant de dureté, esclave des plus petites obligations et délié des pactes les plus sacrés,' the same deviation that transfers moral scruple onto pure questions of form.
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage unmasks a real shallowness beneath the duke's social polish: rigorous about trivial social forms yet released from the most sacred bonds, a pointed if partly sympathetic diminishment.

appraisal_events.evidence: The narrator later understood that the Guermantes considered him of a different 'race,' one that stirred their envy because he possessed merits he was unaware of and which they professed to value above all — though 'cette profession de foi n'était qu'à demi sincère,' disdain and astonishment coexisting with the admiration and envy.
appraisal_events.explanation: The Guermantes are shown secretly admiring and envying the narrator for unrecognized personal merit, even as that admiration is qualified as only half sincere and mixed with condescension.

appraisal_events.evidence: Prince Gilbert, husband of 'Marie-Gilbert,' held outdated notions of rank — seating his wife to his left in the carriage because she was of lesser, though still royal, blood — and 'était une exception et faisait, absent, l'objet des railleries de la famille et d'anecdotes toujours nouvelles.'
appraisal_events.explanation: Prince Gilbert's antiquated snobbery about rank makes him a standing object of his own family's ridicule, a clear local diminishment.

status_effects.explanation: The princesse de Parme's sincere private conviction that everything in the duchesse's household is superior elevates her local standing as a figure of taste.
Beneath his touching gentleness, the passage exposes a revolting hardness and a devotion to form over genuine sentiment or sacred bonds.
The Guermantes are said to envy and half-admire him for merits he did not know he had, even though the passage flags this admiration as only partly sincere.
He is explicitly mocked behind his back by his own family for his outdated, exaggerated notions of rank.

ambiguities: The Guermantes' admiration and envy of the narrator (E3) is explicitly qualified as only half sincere, coexisting with disdain and astonishment, which tempers how positively this event should be read.
